title: The lag that wouldn't drop
outcome: Lag kept growing, the team doubled the consumers, six of them sat idle, and the database got slower.

content.bookmark: In a consumer group each partition has one owner, so the partition count caps how many consumers can work. Find what is slow before adding consumers.

check.prompt: A topic has 6 partitions and a group has 12 consumers. How many consumers receive records?
check.why: Each partition is consumed by exactly one member of a group at a time, so at most 6 members have work.

options: The time since the last record
The log-end offset minus the group's committed offset for that partition
The number of consumers in the group
check.why: The tool shows CURRENT-OFFSET (committed), LOG-END-OFFSET and LAG, the difference, per partition.

check.prompt: Lag grows on every partition evenly, and each consumer is busy waiting on database writes. What helps most?
options: Making each consumer's processing faster, for example by batching the database writes
check.why: The bottleneck is the work per record. Extra consumers past the partition count idle; below it, they add load to the same slow database.

check.prompt: Which Kafka 4.2+ feature lets more consumers than partitions share the work?
options: Share groups, which acknowledge records one by one and give up per-partition ordering
check.why: In a share group, consumers share partitions cooperatively, so there can be more consumers than partitions. The cost is ordering within a partition.

caseStudy.setting: A ride-hailing company (fictional) streams trip-completed events to a trips topic with 6 partitions. A billing consumer group of 6 instances reads each trip and writes a fare row to a relational database, one insert per trip.

events.what: Evening demand doubles. Lag on trips climbs steadily on all six partitions.
The on-call engineer scales the billing group from 6 to 12 instances. Lag keeps climbing.
The database team reports connection pressure and slower inserts. Six of the new instances show no assigned partitions.

pipeline: Billing group · scaled from 6 to 12 instances
Each record · one INSERT into the fares database
Commit · after each poll's records are written
tasks: Why didn't doubling the consumers help?
What would actually bring the lag down?

debrief.title: Why more consumers didn't help
text: With 6 partitions, at most 6 members of a group can be assigned work. The 6 new instances joined, triggered a rebalance, and received nothing.

The real limit was the database: each consumer spent most of its time waiting for single-row inserts. The new instances that did get partitions after the rebalance only added connections to the same database.

debrief.title: What brings lag down
text: Make each consumer faster: write a poll's records to the database in one batch, instead of one insert per record.
If one consumer per partition is truly at its limit, more partitions raise the ceiling, sized with headroom and planned, because adding them moves keys (scenario 4).
If per-partition order doesn't matter for this work, a share group (production-ready since 4.2) allows more consumers than partitions.

debrief.title: Reading lag correctly
text: Lag that grows evenly on all partitions points to slow processing or too little parallelism. Lag on one partition only points to a hot key (scenario 8) or a stuck record (scenario 9).
The consumer's own records-lag-max metric is based on its current position, not the committed offset, so it can differ from the tool's LAG column.

takeaway: The partition count caps a group's parallelism.
Find the slow step before adding consumers.
Even lag says slow work; lag on one partition says a hot key or a stuck record.
content.honesty: If you haven't tuned a lagging consumer, say so and explain how you'd diagnose it. If you have, lead with what the bottleneck turned out to be.

tasks: What questions would you ask before approving more instances?
What should the team commit to measuring?

debrief.title: Questions
text: "Is lag the same on every partition or concentrated on one?" That separates slow work from a hot key.
"What is each consumer waiting on?" That finds the bottleneck.

debrief.title: Measures
text: Time from trip end to fare recorded, with a target.
Throughput per consumer before and after any change.

sayIt.question: Billing fell behind during a peak. How would you work with the team to fix it?
points: Ask for the shape of the lag before any fix.
Ask what the slow step is.
Know the ceiling: more consumers than partitions do nothing.
Agree a measurable target, like time from trip to fare.
Prefer the fix that addresses the bottleneck over adding capacity.

tasks: How do you plan capacity for the next peak?

debrief.title: Impact
text: Fares recorded late may delay receipts and driver payouts. Check whether either was affected and tell drivers if payouts slip.

debrief.title: Planning
text: Agree peak volumes with the business, test billing at twice that, and size partitions and database capacity together.

sayIt.question: How would you plan capacity for a known demand peak?
points: Get peak volumes from the business, with growth.
Test the whole path, including the database, at a multiple of peak.
Size Kafka partitions and downstream capacity together.
Watch time-to-processed as the customer-facing measure.
Review after the peak.

tasks: What do you do during the incident?

debrief.title: During the incident
text: Scale back to 6 instances to stop pointless rebalances and database load.
Agree with the database team whether a quick batching change or more database capacity is faster tonight.

debrief.title: Runbook
text: Check lag per partition first. Never scale a group beyond its partition count. Check downstream latency before scaling up.

sayIt.question: A consumer group is falling behind. Walk me through your first steps.
points: Look at lag per partition: even, or on one?
Check consumers' processing time and what they wait on.
Know that consumers beyond the partition count idle.
Coordinate with downstream owners before adding load.
Record the steps in a runbook.

tasks: How do you speed up the consumer?
When would you add partitions or use a share group?

debrief.title: Speeding it up
text: Batch the inserts per poll, inside one database transaction, and commit offsets after it succeeds.
Tune max.poll.records with the batch size, keeping each poll's work inside max.poll.interval.ms.

debrief.title: Partitions or a share group
text: More partitions if one consumer per partition is at its limit and order per trip still matters; plan it.
A share group if order doesn't matter and you want to scale consumers freely; records are acknowledged one by one.

sayIt.question: How do you scale Kafka consumption, and what limits it?
points: Parallelism within a group is capped by the partition count.
Diagnose before scaling: lag shape, processing time, downstream latency.
Make each consumer efficient: batch downstream writes.
Add partitions with headroom when the per-partition ceiling is reached, knowing keys move.
Share groups (4.2+) allow more consumers than partitions at the cost of ordering.
